anomaly_def.Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level SQL or transaction design forces the engine to scan or change more data than business logic really requires.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead logging path (log buffer, log files, flush, archive, replication retention) becomes the primary bottleneck for commits.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Database processes consume an abnormally high share of CPU, saturating host cores and slowing all work.

When these three root causes are active together the system exhibits extreme and unpredictable latency spikes: statements linger in the slow-query log while commit calls block behind log-flush waits; CPU utilisation stays near 100 %, with long run-queues and scheduler waits; log files grow and switch rapidly yet archiver or replication threads fall behind, triggering "log file full" or "cannot allocate next log" conditions; application timeouts, deadlocks, and recovery-driven crashes become more frequent because transactions remain open for extended periods and hold locks longer than expected. Diagnostic views simultaneously show top SQL by CPU time, high redo generation rates, and dominant log-related wait events, making single-factor analysis inconclusive.

Causally, inefficient workload logic produces oversized scans, updates, and long-lived transactions that explode redo volume and CPU demand. The surge in redo overwhelms the transaction-log subsystem; flush and archive stalls delay commits, which in turn keep transactions—and their locks—open even longer. While sessions wait for log space, they continue to consume CPU in spin-loops, context switching, or retry logic, driving further CPU saturation. The oversubscribed CPU then slows both query execution and the log writer/archiver threads, deepening log congestion. This feedback loop between bad SQL semantics, log pressure, and CPU exhaustion amplifies each individual anomaly, rapidly degrading overall OLTP throughput and stability.

entry.official_definition: Specifies the timeout in seconds for attempts to acquire metadata locks.
entry.trigger_condition: A statement waits longer than lock_wait_timeout while attempting to acquire a metadata lock.
entry.workload_impact: The metadata lock acquisition fails and the statement does not proceed.
entry.default_behavior: Defined as a MySQL server system variable.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when a statement cannot obtain the required lock within the configured waiting window because another transaction or metadata operation is holding an incompatible lock.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect blocking sessions, reduce conflicting transaction overlap, shorten transaction lifetime, and review lock scheduling and schema-change timing.
